title: Reviewed exception: innerhtml-bare-var in docs/assets/hire.js
content: Verified 2026-07-20 on PR #234: every real call site of the local fail()/set() helpers in docs/assets/hire.js passes either a hardcoded string literal or a value already wrapped in escapeHtml() before reaching the innerHTML assignment inside the helper (e.g. set(`Payment failed: ${escapeHtml(msg.slice(0, 200))}`, ...) at lines 268/430; set(`Enter ${escapeHtml(f.label.toLowerCase())}.`, ...) at line 393) — confirmed via grep across every fail(/set( call site in the file, not assumed. code_lint.py cannot trace this because the escaping happens one call frame away from the innerHTML assignment itself (an interprocedural blind spot the checker's own docstring already documents). False positive in THIS file only — a bare innerHTML assignment in any other file still needs the same verification before being waved off.

title: Auto-distilled skill files can arrive wrapped in a stray code fence
content: skillforge/synthesize.py asked its LLM call for "GitHub markdown for a single skills/*.md file" but did not guard against the LLM wrapping the entire response in a fenced code block plus YAML frontmatter — inconsistent with every other file in skillforge/skills/ (plain "# Skill: Title" heading, no fence). Same failure mode agents/builder.py._extract_code_block() already guards against for code files; synthesize.py now strips a leading/trailing fence the same way. Any new LLM-output-to-file pipeline in this repo should assume the model may add an unrequested fence and strip it defensively rather than trusting the raw output.

title: Major-version CDN bumps flagged by check_site_versions.py are often safe to verify quickly
content: Issue: FontAwesome 6.5.1 -> 7.3.1 flagged as "needs manual review" (any major bump is flagged categorically, not because it is known-risky). Actual review: grepped every fa-* class used in docs/ and confirmed all are stable "Classic" style icon names (solid/brands) that FA7 kept fully backward compatible — FA7's breaking changes were in the newer Sharp/Duotone/Chisel families, not Classic. Bumped directly. General pattern for the next major-bump issue this checker files: grep the actual call sites for the library's exported names/classes used in this repo before assuming a major bump is risky — most CDN majors are backward compatible for the narrow surface a small static site actually touches.

title: Per-incident threat analyses were thin because research was thin, not because the LLM was weak
content: User flagged intel/threat-analysis/2026-07-16-defituna-lending.md as saying no public writeups found" for an incident a direct Grok query resolved in full (tx hash, attacker addresses, CertiK-sourced root cause). Root cause: agents/hack_agent.py grounded every report in exactly one Tavily/Brave pre-fetched search (4 results) and never gave the LLM its own live search — a direct chat query to the same underlying model has live web/X search by default; our API call did not. Fixed: agents/llm.py now supports search=True, which adds xAI Live Search (search_parameters) to the payload — but ONLY when the call actually reaches the xai_1 provider (silently absent for every other provider, so safe to pass on any ask()/acall). hack_agent.py now runs two differently-worded pre-fetch searches (was one) AND passes search=True. General lesson: any narrative-generation call site whose output reads thin should be checked for whether its RESEARCH INPUT is thin before assuming the model itself is the limitation — the model was never the bottleneck here.

title: A capability fix scoped to one caller should be checked against every sibling caller of the same shared function
content: search=True (xAI Live Search) was added to agents/llm.py to fix agents/hack_agent.py reporting thin threat analyses. The fix landed correctly scoped (search is a no-op unless the call reaches the xai_1 provider) but was initially wired into only one of ~15 real narrative-generating call sites that share the exact same ask_oci_grok_safe/ask_oci_grok_frontier/grok_analysis() fallback chain. User had to explicitly ask for the rollout to be repo-wide before the other sweeps (security/base/sentiment/macro/virtuals), investigate.py, scout.py, deep_dive_audit.py, external_audit.py, acp_fulfill.py, bounty_ops.py, skillforge_build.py, and agents/run.py's main bounty-report generator got the same fix. General lesson: when a new capability is added to a shared low-level helper (agents/llm.py::ask()) to fix one caller's symptom, grep for every OTHER caller of that same helper chain before considering the fix done — a fix scoped correctly at the mechanism level can still be scoped too narrowly at the rollout level. Exceptions are legitimate (pure code-generation/code-review call sites, and memory-only distillation that should not reach beyond its given inputs) but should be an explicit, stated decision, not an oversight from stopping at the first caller that motivated the fix.

title: Expert assessment disagreed with DAI (0x50c57259) verdict REJECT (45/100)
content:
This is the canonical bridged DAI on Base (an OP Stack L2), deployed as an OptimismMintableERC20. The contract's mint capability and the specific owner address (0x4200...0010) are not anomalies but standard artifacts of the L2 bridge architecture: the owner is a pre-deployed system contract that the official cross-domain messenger uses to mint/burn when DAI moves between L1 and Base. The 382k-holder distribution, 1000+ days of trading, and 704-day DefiLlama pricing history line up exactly with Base's own launch timeline and the role as the dominant stablecoin on that chain. Liquidity and volume figures are modest because this is a low-fee DEX quote rather than a primary venue, but the price peg and absence of any honeypot or proxy flags are consistent with a production bridged stablecoin rather than a custom issuance.

The rule-based score overweighted the generic "owner can change balances" and "mintable" flags without connecting them to the contract's verified name and the known OP Stack pattern; those risks are real for arbitrary but are the intended, audited behavior here. It also underweighted the independent longevity signals (DefiLlama + on-chain age) that would normally filter out short-lived rugs. The cited AFX incident is a false parallel—AFX was a privately keyed bridge, not a system-owned OP Stack mint.

Next check: confirm the owner address against Base's official L1 bridge contracts (or the L2CrossDomainMessenger) to verify it is the expected system address rather than an EOA or upgradeable proxy that could be hijacked.

title: Expert assessment disagreed with axlUSDC (0xEB466342) verdict REJECT (23/100)
content:
This is Axelar Network's canonical bridged USDC implementation on Base (chain 8453), not a standalone project. The contract name, mint/burn mechanics, and 1467-day DefiLlama price history line up exactly with how Axelar has operated its gateway since 2022: validators mint axlUSDC on destination chains when USDC is locked on the source, and burn on the reverse. The 83k-holder base and 937+ days of clean trading further match the pattern of a bridge asset that has seen organic adoption rather than a fresh launch.

The risk factors do not contradict this picture; they are the expected operational surface of any live bridge. Mintability and owner-controlled balance changes are required for cross-chain inflows/outflows, and the single owner address is the Axelar gateway contract itself (not an anonymous EOA). Top-holder concentration is likewise normal for a wrapped stablecoin where liquidity pools, bridges, and custodians sit at the top. The zero locked liquidity is the same story: bridge rarely lock LP because the "liquidity" is the bridge reserves, not a DEX pool that can be rugged.

The rule-based score overweighted generic mint/owner flags without weighting the independent corroboration (DefiLlama first-seen date, verified non-factory source, and absence of any incident in nearly four years). It underweighted the specific threat correlation it cited: the AFX incident was a private-key compromise on a different bridge; Axelar's validator set and gateway have no matching public exploit history in the evidence.

Next concrete check: query the owner address [ADDRESS] on Axelar's own docs or on-chain governance to confirm it is the current gateway contract (or a known multisig) rather than an unclaimed EOA.

title: Expert assessment disagreed with LGNS (0x8f3Cf7ad) verdict PROCEED (92/100)
content:
The evidence paints LGNS as a Polygon child-chain proxy (UChildERC20Proxy) for an asset called Longinus, with unusually deep Quickswap liquidity and nearly 4 million holders. Those two facts together suggest either a heavily adopted bridged stable or a major wrapped that has seen real usage since at least the 2022-era DefiLlama first-seen date. However, the same evidence immediately contradicts itself on price ($2.00 market vs $0.9998 DefiLlama), on asset class (Longinus vs “major stablecoin”), and on supply concentration (top-10 wallets holding 62 %). A legitimate bridged stablecoin would not show a $2 market price or be labeled Longinus; conversely, a non-stable would not be described with a $557 M pegged circulating supply. The proxy pattern itself is standard for Polygon bridges, but the absence of any owner, mint, or tax flags does not resolve the mismatch—it only means the controlling contract sits elsewhere (the root on Ethereum or the bridge admin).

The rule-based score overweighted raw holder count and liquidity depth while underweighting the internal inconsistency between market data and the “stablecoin” narrative; those two data sources cannot both be accurate for the same contract. The concentration flag is noted but not connected to the proxy nature: if the top wallets are bridge escrows or market-maker contracts, 62 % is normal; if they are unidentified EOAs, it is a red flag the score does not resolve.

Next step: resolve the proxy by fetching the implementation address and the Ethereum L1 root (if any) to determine exactly what asset is being bridged and who controls minting.

title: Expert assessment disagreed with LPT (0x289ba170) verdict CAUTION (58/100)
content:
The evidence paints a coherent picture of Livepeer (LPT), the established governance and staking for a decentralized video-transcoding network that launched its mainnet in 2018. The 2785-day DefiLlama price history, 260k+ holders, 1612+ days of incident-free trading, and custom verified contract on Arbitrum all line up with an operating protocol that has real usage and independent third-party tracking rather than a short-lived launch. The mintable flag and 99% top-holder concentration are not contradictions here; they are consistent with Livepeer’s documented (inflationary rewards issued via on-chain governance and staking contracts) and the fact that major holders are typically exchanges, the Livepeer treasury multisig, and liquidity pools rather than anonymous insiders. Liquidity being fully unlocked is also unsurprising for a this old that trades on both Uniswap and centralized venues.

The rule-based score overweighted the generic “mintable + concentrated + unlocked LP” checklist items without connecting them to the project’s actual age and on-chain governance structure; those same flags would be far more concerning on a 30-day-old contract with an EOA owner. It simultaneously underweighted the combination of custom (non-factory) verified source code, zero taxes, and multi-year DefiLlama corroboration, which together are strong signals the deployer is not an anonymous rug team.

Next step: pull the top 10 non-LP holder addresses and cross-reference them against known Livepeer treasury, staking, and exchange wallets (or run a simple label lookup) to confirm whether the apparent concentration is protocol-driven or still controlled by a small set of entities.
